Aug 25 (Reuters) - A U.S. judge on Tuesday blocked an Ohio law requiring residents to present documentary proof of citizenship when registering to vote at the battleground state's motor vehicles offices, in the latest ‌setback for allies of President Donald Trump pushing to tighten voter registration rules.

The decision by Cleveland-based U.S. District Judge ‌Solomon Oliver Jr. marked a defeat for Ohio's Republican government ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. A competitive race for a Senate seat in the ​state is considered critical for Democrats' hopes of winning control of the Senate.

Trump and fellow Republicans in state governments across the country are pushing more restrictions on voter registration, based in part on claims of widespread voting by non-U.S. citizens. Democrats and voting rights advocates counter that non-U.S. citizen voting is rare and that greater restrictions can make it harder for U.S. citizens to vote.

In Ohio, Governor Mike ‌DeWine last year signed a new law requiring ⁠people to present documents such as a birth certificate, a passport or a naturalization certificate when registering to vote while applying for a driver's license or another type of state identification document.

Advocacy groups including the Ohio Alliance for Retired Americans sued to challenge the law, arguing that it imposed an unnecessary obstacle to registering to vote in violation of the National Voter Registration Act, a 1993 federal law that sought to expand voter registration in part by ​requiring states ​to give people the opportunity to register to vote when they ​apply for driver's licenses.

In issuing a preliminary injunction on ‌Tuesday siding with the advocacy groups, Oliver wrote that having voters attest in writing that they are U.S. citizens was enough to allow Ohio election officials to assess their eligibility to vote.

The judge, an appointee of Democratic President Bill Clinton, wrote that NVRA had succeeded in expanding voter registration.

Ben Stafford, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said in a statement, "Eligible Ohioans will now have the opportunity to register to vote at the BMV without having to produce unnecessary paperwork."

Stafford's firm, Elias Law Group, frequently represents the Democratic Party in ‌court.

The office of Ohio's attorney general, which is representing ​the state in court, did not immediately respond to a request for ​comment.

After the lawsuit was filed, Secretary of State Frank LaRose, ​Ohio's top election official, said in a statement, "It's common sense that only U.S. citizens should be on ‌our voter rolls. I won't apologize for, or back ​down from the work we ​do to ensure the integrity of our voter rolls."

Trump has unsuccessfully pushed Congress to pass a nationwide law, known as the SAVE Act, that would require Americans to provide proof of citizenship when registering to vote, arguing it would ​deliver Republicans a "guaranteed" win in November.

A Reuters investigation ‌in July undercut Trump's portrayal of non-U.S. citizen voting as part of a broad Democratic Party conspiracy, finding ​that federal prosecutors have charged just 129 people under a federal "voting by aliens" statute created by Congress in ​1996.

(Reporting by Luc Cohen in New York; Editing by Alistair Bell)

articles.title: ICE arrests jumped to nearly 50,000 in July, the highest monthly total of Trump’s second term
articles.summary: The spike in immigration arrests shows that the administration has continued to advance its mass deportations agenda despite a shift in approach earlier this...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested nearly 50,000 people in July , the highest single monthly arrest total during the second Trump administration, according to new figures.

The spike in immigration arrests shows that the administration has continued to advance its mass deportations agenda despite a shift in approach earlier this year from high-profile operations in large American cities that sparked a public outcry to arrests that have garnered less attention but have nonetheless been disruptive.

The July arrest tally of 49,571 marks a 15% jump from 43,021 arrests a month earlier and a 70% increase from 29,241 in February, in the aftermath of the Trump administration's enforcement surge in Minnesota, according to government data that was provided by ICE to the Deportation Data Project based at U.C. Berkeley and UCLA and analyzed by The Associated Press.

As part of the surging arrest numbers over recent weeks and bolstered by a hiring surge , ICE has made arrests at traffic stops. The agency has increasingly relied on state and local law enforcement partners who are assuming immigration enforcement duties. And ICE officers have started to arrest people from Haiti who've seen their protections from deportation stripped away.

The new arrest numbers show the administration "didn't stop the enforcement," said Mark Krikorian of the Center for Immigration Studies, which advocates for more immigration restrictions.

"They changed the tactics and are, if anything, being more effective."

State partnerships becoming key to immigration enforcement

Immigration arrests the month before President Donald Trump returned to office hovered a little over 8,000, a figure largely made up of immigrants transferred from city or state jails and prisons and turned over to ICE to remove from the country. During Trump's first year back in office, the numbers started climbing as the administration loosened restrictions on where and whom ICE could arrest while it also infused the agency with billions of dollars.

By December, the number of arrests jumped to more than 40,177, according to the data, which was obtained through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit. Homeland Security largely stopped reporting immigration enforcement data at the beginning of the second Trump administration, making the data from the Deportation Data Project one of the few insights into how the agency is operating.

In the aftermath of two fatal shootings in Minnesota in January that sparked protests and an uproar from Democratic lawmakers, arrests began to fall in February. After remaining stagnant for months, the numbers surged in June and then again in July.

The number of arrests made by state and local police departments who partner with ICE has dramatically increased over the last year. Those partnerships, which ICE has grown with the help of generous financial incentives for participating agencies, accounted for 6,500 arrests in July, or about 13% of the total, the data showed. A year earlier, they accounted for less than 5% of ICE's monthly arrests.

Texas and Florida accounted for nearly 20,000 of the July arrests, in a sign of how important those states have become to the Trump administration's mass deportation agenda. Both states have leaned heavily into those cooperation deals with ICE, known as 287g agreements, that allow local and state law enforcement to essentially operate as arms of federal immigration enforcement.

That close cooperation is increasingly resulting in arrests like one last week in Florida's Key West. The manager at the Half Shell Raw Bar said Tuesday that one of his staff members, a 36-year-old asylum seeker who fled Haiti in 2017 after receiving death threats, was arrested by local police and turned over to ICE.

The manager, Bobby Kuchinsky, said the man had worked as a cook and supervisor at the restaurant and was the main provider of his family. Kuchinsky declined to identify the man out of concern for his safety while in custody.

"He was an excellent worker, he learned very fast, he never had any problem with the law," Kuchinsky said in an interview with the AP, noting that it will be a challenge to replace him. "He was a nice kid, he was a family man."

DHS secretary pledged a quieter approach but mass deportations still a priority

In his confirmation hearing earlier this year, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin pledged to keep ICE out of the headlines, suggesting that the administration's immigration crackdown might take a softer approach. But his tenure has been marred by a number of fatal shootings of immigrants in encounters with ICE officers. And the figures show Mullin hasn't shifted the agency from Trump's vision for mass deportations.

Under Mullin's predecessor, Kristi Noem, immigration enforcement was often characterized by high-profile operations that targeted specific Democratic cities such as Chicago, Los Angeles and Minneapolis. Operations, often led by former Border Patrol agent Greg Bovino, were blasted out on social media videos showing officers bursting out of moving vans to chase people or rappelling from helicopters onto apartment rooftops.

But Krikorian said those tactics were "provoking a lot of ordinary people, turning them off even if they liked the idea of the immigration law being enforced."

New data shows most immigrants arrested didn't have criminal history

The administration has often said its immigration enforcement operations target people who have committed crimes in the U.S. and as a way to make the country safer.

But the data shows that more than half of those arrested in July had not been convicted of any crimes and were not facing any criminal charges. Less than a quarter of those arrested had been convicted of a crime.

And half of the arrests were non-custodial, which means ICE agents arrested people in the community rather than someone already behind bars or held by local police.

Patricia Quiñonez, a journalist at Utahzolanos, which covers the Venezuelan immigrant community in Utah, said immigration arrests during traffic stops have increased sharply in recent months.

"They stop you for whatever reason — for example, you don't have a driver's license, your vehicle tags are expired, your windows are more tinted than what is allowed. From there, they take advantage of the situation and ask about immigration."

People with valid work permits and pending asylum claims are among those arrested, said Quiñonez, who believes they are being targeted by race.

Salomon reported from Miami, Sullivan from Minneapolis and Foley from Iowa City, Iowa. Associated Press writer Elliot Spagat in San Diego contributed.

articles.title: Shapiro holds 16-point lead in reelection bid polling
articles.summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) is cruising toward reelection, according to a new poll of likely voters in the Keystone State. The latest survey from The New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena University showed 55 percent of respondents supported Shapiro in the gubernatorial race. Another 39 percent backed GOP state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, and 6 percent did…
articles.body:
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) is cruising toward reelection, according to a new poll of likely voters in the Keystone State.

The latest survey from The New York Times/Philadelphia Inquirer/Siena University showed 55 percent of respondents supported Shapiro in the gubernatorial race. Another 39 percent backed GOP state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, and 6 percent did not choose either candidate or refused to answer.

Shapiro’s edge over Garrity among Pennsylvanians of multiple backgrounds is apparent based on the data.

The incumbent governor leads among men, women, likely white voters, likely Black voters and the four age groups the survey split respondents into: ages 18-29, 30-44, 45-64 and 65-plus. He also holds a 34-point lead over Garrity among voters with a college degree and a 4-point edge among those without one, according to the poll.

That includes a whopping 72-point lead among nonwhite respondents without a college degree — while Garrity leads by 5 points among white respondents without a degree.

In 2022, Shapiro won his first election to the governor’s mansion by nearly 15 points over GOP state Sen. Doug Mastriano.

Less than two years after that race, the Pennsylvania governor was a finalist in former Vice President Kamala Harris’s search for a running mate in the 2024 presidential election. Harris ultimately selected Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, with the Democratic duo losing to President Trump and Vice President Vance that year.

Shapiro has indicated he is considering a bid for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.

At the annual National Action Network convention in April, the governor said the Democratic Party is undertaking a “debate” that it “hasn’t had for a good long while,” an internal battle he deemed “healthy” for the country.

“What I can tell you for sure is that I want to be a part of that debate,” he told the Rev. Al Sharpton.

Forty-seven percent of 296 respondents, a smaller group, in the survey said they would be “very likely” to back Shapiro for the Democratic nomination in 2028 . About 39 percent said they were somewhat likely to do so, while 9 percent said they were not too likely and 4 percent said they were not at all likely, the numbers show.

The Times/Inquirer/Siena University survey was conducted from Aug.17-21 among 760 respondents. It has a margin of error of 4.6 percentage points.

articles.title: Dem House hopeful defended music video showing woman restrained, groped and killed
articles.summary: Bobby Pulido defended Gerardo Ortiz's graphic music video depicting sexual violence, adding to controversies as he challenges Monica De La Cruz.
articles.body: In a 2016 interview, Latin Grammy Award-winning artist and Democratic congressional candidate Bobby Pulido defended a fellow singer against criticism for a graphic music video that depicted acts of sexual violence and murder. In the video production of "Fuiste Mía" or "You were mine" by Gerardo Ortiz, a singer walks in on his girlfriend cheating on him. After shooting her lover, he then handcuffs her to a pole, blindfolds her, and gropes her before putting her in the trunk of his car and setting it on fire. In response to backlash, Pulido defended Ortiz, calling the video a matter of artistic direction. "I've made videos with suggestive images; some have stayed, others have been edited, and still others were never used. That's the decision of the artist and their team," Pulido said in response to public backlash for the production. Pulido’s resurfaced response to the music video is the latest in a series of controversies Pulido has tried to downplay as he pursues a seat in the U.S. House of Representatives in Texas’ 15th Congressional District — one of the country’s most competitive seats. FORMER DISNEY TEEN STAR EXPOSES CHILLING WARNING SIGNS OF PREDATORY BEHAVIOR IN HOLLYWOOD Pulido is best known for Tejano, or Mexican–Spanish folk-style, songs like "Desvelado" and "Se Murió de Amor," and received five nominations for a Latin Grammy Awards, winning Best Tejano Album in 2025 and 2022. He filed to run for Congress in Texas’ 15th district, challenging Rep. Monica De La Cruz, R-Texas. A two-term incumbent, she last won election to the district in 2024 in a 57.1% to 42.9% victory over Democratic nominee Michelle Vallejo.  Along the way, Pulido has drawn scrutiny for a resurfaced history of posting links to explicit websites on his personal X account — as well as for a social media post of what appeared to be him urinating on President Donald Trump’s Hollywood Walk of Fame star. Pulido has shrugged off criticism for both, stating in 2024 that it's "it’s impossible to have Twitter and not watch porn," and that he had only poured water on Trump’s star as a joke. More notably, Pulido has also had to fend off criticisms of bringing a registered sex offender to a Texas middle school benefit concert in 2018. DEM TIED TO CARTEL OPERATIVE SAYS 'WHITE NATIONALISTS' JOINING IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT TO 'HUNT DOWN PEOPLE' In that case, Pulido denied knowledge of his associate’s status at the time and has dismissed coverage of it as a "nothing story," according to Axios. Similarly, in his defense of Ortiz, Pulido downplayed the music video, arguing that viewers had become accustomed to increasingly graphic images. "What happens when there's a [car] accident?" Pulido asked, comparing the music video to real-life instances of tragedy. "Traffic doesn't flow because people slow down or even stop to see what happened; something similar happens with the regional Mexican genre when these kinds of incidents occur." At least one Republican onlooker is left unconvinced by the defense of the music video — and defenses of other past behaviors. "Bobby Pulido has spent his entire adult life defending perverts and predators while lashing out at members of law enforcement who keep Texans safe. He is a truly sick individual who is morally rotten," Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC), said in a statement to Fox News Digital. DEM RIPPED FOR ‘DISGUSTING’ ABSENCE ON BILL TO PUNISH VIOLENT CRIMINALS AFTER GIRL STRANGLED IN GRISLY KILLING CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Pulido campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment about his defense of the video and whether he had a track record of downplaying potentially problematic conduct.

articles.title: Maxwell’s attempt at freedom ‘deeply troubling’: Survivor
articles.summary: Maxwell is serving a 20-year federal prison sentence for her part in the sex trafficking of minor females.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Ghislaine Maxwell, who was charged as a co-conspirator of disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein, was recently denied a bid to overturn her sexual abuse crimes conviction on Tuesday.

Maxwell, who is serving a 20-year federal prison sentence for her part in the alleged sex trafficking scheme, which involved minors, attempted to have her conviction thrown out earlier this year.

In a motion made public Tuesday, Judge Paul A. Engelmayer ruled Maxwell was unauthorized to file any more requests to toss out her conviction.

The summary read in part, “Maxwell, however, is not to submit any further filings. Any such filings will not be considered.”

Epstein survivor calls Maxwell’s post-conviction activity ‘troubling’

Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell attend de Grisogono Sponsors The 2005 Wall Street Concert Series Benefitting Wall Street Rising, with a Performance by Rod Stewart at Cipriani Wall Street on March 15, 2005 in New York City. (Photo by Joe Schildhorn/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)

After the judge’s decision was made public, former Playboy Playmate Audra Christiansen called Maxwell’s motion to try to overturn her conviction “deeply troubling.”

“For decades, survivors of Jeffrey Epstein’s network fought to be taken seriously. Many were children or very young women like me when they were exploited,” she told NewsNation. “They lived with the consequences while powerful people had access to money, attorneys, influence and institutions that repeatedly failed to protect victims.” “Maxwell now argues that attorneys representing Epstein’s accusers somehow acted as ‘de facto prosecutors’ and that newly released documents prove her due process rights were violated,” Christiansen continued. “A federal judge has rejected those claims, finding that the supposed new evidence was largely irrelevant to her case.”

She accused Epstein of sexual abuse in 2004, and asked Playboy founder Hugh Hefner to report him to the FBI.

Christiansen told NewsNation that after the abuse, Maxwell allegedly threatened her and her family .

On Tuesday, the former playmate said, “The focus cannot continually shift away from the people who were harmed and toward portraying those convicted in this network as its victims.”

“Survivors deserved due process, too. We deserved investigations when we came forward. We deserved institutions that acted when warning signs were raised,” she added. “We deserved transparency, accountability, and protection from people who used wealth and power to avoid consequences.”

Epstein survivors’ attorney calls Maxwell’s motion ‘frivolous’

A document that was included in the U.S. Department of Justice release of the Jeffrey Epstein files, photographed Tuesday, Feb. 3, 2026, shows a U.S. passport renewal in 2012 for Ghislaine Maxwell. (AP Photo/Jon Elswick)

Arick Fudali, who represents 11 Epstein survivors , told NewsNation that Maxwell’s attempts are “frivolous.”

“It was apparently not enough for Ms. Maxwell that she was moved to a minimum-security resort style prison, and she has once again attempted to get her sentence and conviction overturned,” Fudali continued. “I am very pleased to see that those frivolous efforts were rejected, and I agree that her arguments were meritless.”

He added, “Ghislaine Maxwell is a convicted child sex trafficker, and she belongs behind bars for the remainder of her sentence.”

Ghislaine Maxwell’s legal maneuvers behind bars

This is not the first time the convicted sex trafficker has tried to overturn her prison sentence.

In October 2025, the Supreme Court dismissed her bid to overturn the conviction. Epstein’s former girlfriend was convicted in 2021 and arrested in 2019.

In April 2025, her attorney, David Oscar Markus, wrote in their petition to the Supreme Court, “In this case, the government made a written promise that Epstein’s co-conspirators would not be prosecuted by the United States, and Maxwell was in fact prosecuted as a co-conspirator of Epstein by the United States.

He continued, “The only question is whether the government’s promise that the ‘United States’ would not prosecute her was enforceable against the U.S. Attorney’s office in New York, or only against the Southern District of Florida.”

This undated photo released by the U.S. Department of Justice shows Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell. (U.S. Department of Justice via AP)

In August 2025, the Department of Justice released 16 audio recordings and four transcripts from then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche’s meetings with the imprisoned Maxwell on July 24 and 25.

Shortly after Maxwell’s meeting with Blanche, she was moved to a minimum- security prison , Federal Prison Camp Bryan, in Texas.

Diana Falzone is the senior national investigations reporter at NewsNation Digital, covering the federal government, warzones and top-level criminal investigations.

articles.title: Inside Gavin Newsom’s private mansion on sale for $7.5M
articles.summary: The governor is selling the property he lived in during his two terms in office, only months ahead of his leaving the post.
articles.body:
California Governor Gavin Newsom has listed his private mansion in Sacramento for sale for $7.5 million, double the price he and his wife, Jennifer Siebel Newsom, bought it for seven years ago.

The property in Fair Oaks has served as the Democrat's base during his two terms in office, and its sale comes mere months before Newsom officially steps down in January 2027.

Many have speculated about Newsom's possible run for the presidency in 2028, though the governor has not confirmed whether he will be a candidate for the nation's top job or not. The sale of his California home is only likely to fuel rumors there will be an impending presidential campaign announcement.

The Newsoms purchased the 12,000-square-foot Sacramento mansion in 2019 to avoid living in the official governor's mansion, a 150-year-old property, which, until Jerry Brown decided to move into it in 2015, had been serving as a museum. An exception was the stay of Ronald Reagan, who lived there for a few months in 1967.

The mansion at 7640 Tobia Way is only 15 miles from the state Capitol, making it easy for Newsom to commute to work. When the governor bought it as a "more kid-friendly" alternative to the official Victorian home, he paid $3.7 million for it.

That was just before historically low borrowing costs during the pandemic sparked a home-buying frenzy all across the country which, clashing with chronically low inventory levels, sent prices through the roof. We do not know if, since 2019, Newsom has implemented any upgrade or changes to the home.

The mansion, built in 1984, boasts several high-end amenities including a resort-style pool, a private tennis court, a cold plunge pool, and a 5,000-bottle wine cellar with its own tasting room. It has seven bedrooms and nine bathrooms, as well as three partial ones.

The sale is being managed by Matthew Hindy and Nick Sadek with Sotheby's International Realty. "It's a beautiful property. It's been well maintained and holds a special charm," Hindy told Newsweek in a written statement.

The listing describes the property as "an extraordinary showcase of Santa Barbara-inspired architecture […] privately positioned along the bluffs on 8.2 acres, where sweeping views and exceptional privacy create a truly rare setting."

According to the agent, "the residence offers an unparalleled combination of grandeur, comfort, and effortless entertaining."

The home's primary bathroom features two walk-in closets, dual showers and water closets, and a luxurious soaking tub, in what the listing describes as a "spa-like experience."

Outdoors, the home features a private pool, cold plunge, and hot tub. There is also a four-car garage.

"Some homes are beautiful in photographs, but this is one you truly have to see with your own eyes," the listing concludes.

After Newsom ends his term, he and his family are expected to move 90 miles west of the Sacramento home to Kentfield, Marin County, where they bought a home in 2024 for $9 million. Politico reported in 2024 that all four of the Newsoms' children were being enrolled in Marin County schools that year.

The family already lived in a different home in Kentfield before Newsom's electoral victory in 2018.

Newsweek contacted Newsom's office for comment by email on Tuesday morning.

Izzy Garson, a spokesperson for Newsom, told SFGate that "with the Governor's term ending in January 2027, the family began a gradual transition in 2024, purchasing a home in Marin County to provide continuity for their children's education. The sale of their Sacramento home is the next step in that transition."

Newsom is leaving office because, due to term limits, he cannot run for reelection. It is unclear who will succeed the Democratic governor in his Sacramento home—or in office, for that matter. The Golden State will hold an election to choose his successor on November 3, with Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton running.

Becerra currently leads Hilton 49.2 percent to 41 percent among 912 registered voters, with 9.8 percent undecided, according to a recent survey conducted August from 14 to 16 . The poll was commissioned by Hilton's campaign and conducted by David Wolfson, a pollster and faculty member in Columbia University's Political Analytics graduate program. It carries a 3.3-point margin of error and used MMS text-to-web methodology.

articles.title: Watchdog files bar complaint against Jeanine Pirro over bid to indict 6 Democratic lawmakers
articles.summary: A legal watchdog says it filed bar complaints on Tuesday accusing U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro and two lieutenants of violating their ethical duties in seekin...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A legal watchdog says it filed bar complaints on Tuesday accusing U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro and two lieutenants of violating their ethical duties in seeking to charge six Democratic lawmakers with federal crimes for appearing in a video that called on troops to resist unlawful orders.

The Legal Accountability Center's bar complaints , filed in New York and Virginia, claim Pirro and her subordinates, Carlton Davis and Steven Vandervelden , abused their prosecutorial powers to seek "meritless" indictments against President Donald Trump's "perceived political enemies."

Tim Lauer, a spokesperson for Pirro's Washington-based office, noted that it's a grand jury's job — not prosecutors' — to decide whether to hand up an indictment.

"Attempting to weaponize the disciplinary process against prosecutors for doing their jobs amounts to nothing more than a frivolous complaint," Lauer said in a statement.

In February, a grand jury in Washington refused to indict Sens. Mark Kelly and Elissa Slotkin and four House Democrats for urging U.S. service members to follow established military protocols and reject orders they believe to be unlawful. All six lawmakers previously served in the military or at intelligence agencies. Trump accused them of sedition "punishable by DEATH" in a social media post.

A grand jury's refusal to return an indictment is extraordinarily rare, but it has become increasingly common in Washington during Trump's second term. Pirro's critics have accused her of pursuing other legally dubious and politically motivated cases at the Republican president's behest, such as the recently abandoned felony charge against a former Olympian who was accused of defacing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

The center has filed complaints against other Trump administration officials , including Ed Martin Jr. , Pirro's predecessor as U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia. Martin has been a leading figure in Trump's campaign to use the Justice Department to prosecute his political opponents.

In its complaint against Pirro, the center asks bar officials to investigate whether she and her colleagues violated rules of professional conduct for attorneys — and to "pursue appropriate discipline" against them. Its complaint against Pirro says her office had no legal basis for its "patently improper effort" to secure an indictment against the six lawmakers.

"The only purpose could have been political animus and a desire to intimidate perceived enemies of the federal government and the President, who personally criticized the lawmakers' video as seditious and punishable by death," the complaint says.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has tried to punish Kelly , a former Navy pilot representing Arizona, for participating in the video. Kelly sued in federal court to block the censure from Hegseth. A district court judge ruled in his favor . Hegseth has asked an appeals court to review the decision.

The center filed its complaint against Pirro and Vandervelden with a grievance committee based in White Plains, New York. In New York, the state Supreme Court's appellate division governs ethical complaints against attorneys. The center filed its complaint against Davis with the Virginia State Bar.

"Prosecutors have enormous power, and with that power comes an obligation to exercise independent legal judgment rather than use the criminal justice system to carry out a president's political demands," the center's co-founder, Michael Teter, said in a statement.

Pirro, who served as a county prosecutor and judge in New York, left her Fox News hosting job to become the top federal prosecutor for Washington last year.

articles.title: How Trump can fix Puerto Rico’s broken infrastructure
articles.summary: Former Gov. Luis Fortuño argues that the Federal Oversight and Management Board must replace its current mainland members with local leaders to resolve PREPA’s decade-long bankruptcy and address Puerto Rico’s critical infrastructure failures.
articles.body:
Puerto Rico is facing its worst drought in nearly 100 years this summer. The majority of San Juan, Puerto Rico’s capital, is now under severe water rationing due to aging and poorly maintained water infrastructure that is incapable of handling the severe drought conditions. The current water crisis is only the latest manifestation of Puerto Rico’s infrastructure deficiencies. Unfortunately, Puerto Rico has been dealing with an electricity infrastructure failure for decades. Examining why electricity reliability hasn’t improved over the past 10 years despite immense federal supervision from the Federal Oversight and Management Board for Puerto Rico holds the key to solving Puerto Rico’s infrastructure challenges.

In 2016, Congress created the oversight panel to oversee Puerto Rico’s economic recovery. For the last 10 years, it has kept the territory’s sole provider of electricity, with the Puerto Rico Electric Power Company, known as PREPA, in a perpetual state of bankruptcy. This decision impairs both reliable power for Puerto Rico’s residents and the island’s future economic growth.

How could this happen? The short answer is that the current members of the federal oversight board charged with getting PREPA out of bankruptcy do not live in Puerto Rico. They do not experience firsthand the consequences of decisions that delay much-needed investment in the power grid to improve reliability upon PREPA’s exit from bankruptcy. Last August, President Trump dismissed six of the seven oversight board members for being ineffective at resolving the PREPA bankruptcy. Three of those dismissed members are prolonging the inevitable by challenging these dismissals in court .

The people of Puerto Rico deserve better. The solution seems obvious. PREPA needs capital to improve electric service for customers. Electric utilities depend on assets with long useful lives, such as power plants. Standard practice is to finance long-term assets with long-term debt, which spreads the cost to ratepayers over an extended period. Otherwise, today’s customers pay in full for assets today that will benefit future generations of ratepayers. PREPA’s existing bondholder investors, who comprise most of the municipal finance market, have already offered billions to PREPA to this end. The governor of Puerto Rico has also indicated that over $13 billion in Puerto Rico’s cash balance account could be part of a broad solution.

The result is a worst-case scenario for the people of Puerto Rico. Critical modernization efforts to the electric grid are delayed, all while current customers bear the cost of capital improvements that should be financed and pay high electric rates for unreliable and inadequate service.

Rather than resolve PREPA’s bankruptcy, the board has wasted over half a billion dollars of Puerto Rican taxpayers’ money on high-priced New York attorneys and consultants who haven’t advanced the bankruptcy case in nearly 10 years.

The current and the previous board chairs are both professors who specialize in teaching corporate bankruptcy law. Neither has real-world expertise in understanding how U.S. public utilities operate or finance themselves. The current board chair has also gone out of his way to reject two previously signed consensual PREPA debt restructuring agreements.

The board wasn’t always like this. When it convened in the summer of 2016, it had strong on-island representation and leadership for the first four years, led by local Puerto Rican businessman Jose Carrion serving as board chair. Through his efforts and those of other on-island board members, Puerto Rico reached largely consensual debt restructuring deals that led to the reduction of Puerto Rico’s government debt by more than $40 billion.

We need on-island business leaders, who have a much better understanding of the island’s needs than mainland bankruptcy professors and academics, to run the board once again.

Both the recent Trump v. Cook and Trump v. Slaughter U.S. Supreme Court rulings support the president’s right to hold the FOMB accountable for its failures, including through exercising the right to fire these officials.

I urge local elected officials to support the Trump administration in first filling the three vacant board seats with qualified individuals capable of solving PREPA’s crisis. Once those seats are filled, and consistent with the Supreme Court’s recent rulings affirming the president’s authority to hold the the board accountable, I urge the administration to terminate the three remaining board members who challenged the president’s decision, none of whom will take the steps needed to free PREPA from bankruptcy.

Luis Fortuño served as governor of Puerto Rico from 2009-2013.

articles.title: Donalds picks state senator as running mate for Florida governor
articles.summary: Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) announced Tuesday that Florida state Sen. Bryan Avila (R) will be his running mate in the Sunshine State’s gubernatorial race. Donalds, who won the GOP primary last week, praised Avila as a “proven warrior” and “conservative fighter.” Avila, the former speaker pro tempore of the Florida House, has represented the state’s…
articles.body:
Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) announced Tuesday that Florida state Sen. Bryan Avila (R) will be his running mate in the Sunshine State’s gubernatorial race.

Donalds, who won the GOP primary last week, praised Avila as a “proven warrior” and “conservative fighter.” Avila, the former speaker pro tempore of the Florida House, has represented the state’s 39th Senate District since November 2022.

“He has fought woke ideology, he’s fought higher taxes, he’s fought higher costs every single day, and I could not be more prouder to have him stand by my side,” Donalds said at an event at the Freedom Tower in downtown Miami.

Avila, the son of Cuban immigrants, resides in the heavily Cuban-influenced city of Hialeah, located in north Miami-Dade County. Miami-Dade is the largest county in Florida, and 29.2 percent of Floridians are Hispanic or Latino, according to 2025 estimates by the U.S. Census Bureau .

The Florida state lawmaker, a captain in the Florida Army National Guard, said it was an “incredible honor” to be the running mate of Donalds.

“Byron, thank you for your trust, thank you for your friendship and thank you for your leadership,” Avila said, with Donalds standing behind him.

The Donalds-Avila pairing will face off against former GOP Rep. David Jolly (Fla.), a converted Democrat who won the party’s gubernatorial nomination last week.

Jolly’s running mate is former Rep. Gwen Graham (D-Fla.), an assistant Education secretary during the Biden administration and the daughter of former Florida Gov. and Sen. Bob Graham (D).

While Jolly has campaigned as a moderate Democrat, Donalds on Tuesday tied him to state Rep. Angie Nixon (D), the party’s Senate nominee . Nixon is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America.

Donalds also called the Jolly-Graham ticket “boring,” a quip that elicited cheers from the crowd.

“They’ve joined forces to create the most boring and uninspiring ticket Florida Democrats could have ever put together,” the Republican nominee remarked.

A Democrat has not won a governor’s race in Florida since 1994, with the state morphing from the largest purple state in the country to a conservative stronghold under Gov. Ron DeSantis (R). DeSantis defeated former Gov. Charlie Crist (D) by nearly 20 points in 2022.

In the statewide primary that concluded last week, more than 1.7 million Republicans and nearly 1.3 million Democrats cast a ballot, according to data from Fresh Take Florida .

Overall, nearly 51 percent of registered Republicans and nearly 38 percent of registered Democrats voted in the primary.

articles.title: James Carville goes nuclear on Jeffries over Jared Kushner sit-down and demands Democrats draw a line
articles.summary: James Carville slammed Hakeem Jeffries for meeting with Jared Kushner, saying Democrats universally agree they don't sit down with Donald Trump's inner circle.
articles.body: Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville tore into House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., on Monday over his meeting with U.S. special envoy Jared Kushner, saying Democrats of every viewpoint agree on one thing: they don't sit down with President Donald Trump's inner circle. The takedown came just days after news broke that Jeffries had sat down with Trump’s son-in-law to discuss housing, immigration and high living costs as possible categories of common ground, The New York Times first reported. "Let me try to explain something," Carville said. "And Hakeem, you’re a smart guy. Let me explain something here, very, very clear. You have Democrats that have a different position on Medicare for all, whether that’s a good idea. You have Democrats that have different positions on effective policing, and there’s a whole variety of subjects of which there are some disagreements within the Democratic Party." HAKEEM JEFFRIES REJECTS MEDICARE FOR ALL, DSA AGENDA AS RO KHANNA CALLS HEALTH PLAN 'MOST IMPORTANT PRIORITY' Despite the seemingly good-faith meeting, Carville told Jeffries that Democrats’ ability to find compromise does not extend across party lines. "On one thing, on one thing, there is no disagreement," he said. "There’s unanimity. And it is simply this: in the opinion of every Democrat in the United States, progressive, moderate, middle road, left, f---, I don’t know whatever you want, we believe one thing above all." CARVILLE UNLOADS ON DSA SOCIALISTS: 'DON'T USE OUR GOD---- NAME' "These people are a pack of felons and traitors, and you do not meet with them. You do not meet with them," Carville continued. Carville went on to offer his own suggestion for what he believes the best course of action would be for Democrats looking to see eye-to-eye with Kushner. "We need to drag [Kushner’s] a-- before a committee and find out what backdoor-dealing, w----house s--- he's got going on with Steve Whitcomb and everybody else," Carville said. "We're not going to be nice to you. We don't like you." Carville also added that Trump and his administration "have no idea what they’re doing," while accusing them of "making every backdoor bulls--- deal they can." CARVILLE WARNS DEMOCRATS MAY NEED TO BLOCK FAR-LEFT CANDIDATES FROM JOINING CAUCUS, MODERATE GROUP DISAGREES CARVILLE TORCHES DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS AS 'PACK OF FOOLS,' PRAISES AOC'S POLITICAL EVOLUTION The veteran strategist ended with a single line of advice to Jeffries: "And we don’t meet with them. Don’t meet with them." In light of the fallout following Jeffries’ meeting with Kushner, Axia CEO Jason Mudd told Fox News Digital the biggest problem Jeffries is facing is the fact that the news of the meeting came out after it had been held. JEFFRIES' SOCIALISM DILEMMA: NEW YORK VICTORIES EXPOSE DEMOCRATIC PARTY DIVIDE "Jeffries got caught being reasonable in private without being strategic in public. To be clear, this isn't about whether Kushner deserved the meeting. It's about how the meeting was handled," Mudd said. "Now Jeffries is explaining it after the leak instead of framing it before the leak. That's the real mistake. Not taking the meeting itself." Mudd went on to acknowledge that politicians often do have to compromise with members of opposing parties, but should do so while remaining transparent with their constituents. The public relations CEO and expert added that to mitigate the fallout, he would suggest Jeffries provide full insight into his meeting with Kushner as a way to regain trust within his party. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If I were advising Jeffries or his camp right now, I'd tell him to stop playing defense and take control of the narrative today," Mudd said. "Say what the meeting was about, why he took it, and what came of it, in his own words. Silence and vague statements read as guilt even when there's nothing to hide, and right now the story is being written for him and without him." Fox News Digital reached out to Jeffries, Kushner and the White House for comment.

articles.title: Trump doesn’t seem to care what people want anymore
articles.summary: When President Donald Trump took the political world by storm in 2016, his rise was often described as a “populist” one. He seems to have abandoned that bran...
articles.body:
When President Donald Trump took the political world by storm in 2016, his rise was often described as a "populist" one. And he certainly played the part of a renegade challenging a broken political system on behalf of regular Americans.

Ten years later, though, Trump has almost completely abandoned this brand of politics.

Indeed, in many ways, he has become the anti-populist .

And he's got the poll numbers to prove it.

Polling this month from Reuters and Ipsos has shown Trump's approval rating dropping to a record low of 33%. That's just 1 in 3 Americans who endorse his job performance.

But perhaps more telling is the still-falling percentage who "strongly" approve of him. It's been dropping for a while now . And in the newest poll, it's at just 13% of all Americans and 35% of Republicans .

That's roughly 1 in 8 Americans who think what Trump is doing is great — a remarkably small number of truly devoted supporters. And despite the president's supposed hammerlock on his base, nearly two-thirds of Republicans are less than enthused.

So how does a president get to that point?

For Trump, it's by almost totally disregarding public opinion in favor of his own whims, desires and even personal enrichment and glorification — a propensity he seems inclined to continue even during the stretch run of the midterms, when many politicians are highly sensitive to what plays well with voters.

Trump's threatened 50% tariffs on Canada are a case in point.

A CNN poll this spring showed 65% of Americans said Trump's tariffs had a negative impact on their personal finances. And even when the tariffs as a whole weren't as unpopular last year, his initial Canada levies were still very unpopular; between 60% and 64% of Americans opposed them from the outset.

So what does Trump do 70 days before the midterms? Embrace a trade war with Canada, naturally.

Trump on Tuesday even threatened to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America as part of the feud — echoing his purported renaming of the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. Around two-thirds of Americans also opposed the latter change.

Vice President JD Vance got in on the act Monday by mislabeling Canada as a "state" and calling it a "Freudian slip" — evoking Trump's threats to make Canada the 51st state. And why not? A Marquette University Law School poll last year, after all, showed 75% of Americans opposed this idea.

Trump's recent positive comments about data centers are also perplexing for a supposed populist.

There is perhaps no more clear-cut populist issue right now than opposing data centers. As many as 7 in 10 Americans oppose having them in their communities, largely perceiving the centers as something powerful tech companies are inflicting upon them.

But even as his fellow Republicans turn sharply against them, Trump is embracing them . He's calling data centers "big, strong, bold, and Money Machines" and "Cash Cows." He said communities should welcome them and praised their architecture as the "most incredible buildings I've ever seen." He's even criticized Republicans for supporting moratoriums that ban data center development.

But these are hardly the only examples of Trump's anti-populism:

Polls show 6 in 10 Americans say Trump has "gone too far" in changing institutions like the Kennedy Center, and just 9% of Americans think it's appropriate to name government buildings after Trump while he's still president. Yet Trump is again trying to slap his name on the Kennedy Center.

He continues to focus extensively on his renovations of DC — often parading them for the cameras like he did with the new White House helipad Monday. This despite a Washington Post poll last month showing Americans viewed these kinds of projects negatively by a 2-to-1 margin.

The Iran war was clearly not what Americans wanted from the start; they opposed intervention by 2-to-1 margins in prewar polls. And Trump's supposed anti-war streak was core to his populism. Yet six months after launching the war, Trump is now threatening to extend the conflict through the midterms.

He's continued his factually deprived assault on vaccines this month, even as KFF polling shows 6 in 10 Americans oppose the administration's handling of the issue.

Trump until a few weeks ago seemingly wouldn't let go of his $1.776 billion "anti-weaponization" fund, which the White House has said could send money to violent January 6, 2021, defendants. This despite a poll last year showing 83% of Americans opposed Trump decision to pardon those people — much less paying them.

The problem with most of those examples isn't just that Trump is focused on his unpopular pet projects. It's that he's focused on them to the exclusion of and often at the expense of what people really want, which is a laser focus on affordability and economic issues.

He instead repeatedly talks about how we're in an economic "golden age," even though just 4% of Americans in the new Reuters-Ipsos poll said the economy was "very strong."

And people have noticed, with polls showing overwhelming majorities believe that he's neglecting the most important issues like inflation.

It all begs the question: What do voters do when a president basically casts off even the veneer of interest in doing what the people want — and instead does a series of things he wants that even large segments of his base appear uncomfortable with ?

It sets up a pretty remarkable test of partisanship in the 2026 midterms.

articles.title: Carville rips Jeffries for meeting with Kushner: ‘We don’t want to f‑‑‑ with them’

articles.body:
Democratic strategist James Carville went after House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) over his recent meeting with President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

“One thing that I know and you know, these are a pack of crooks, and they’re a pack of people that don’t give a s‑‑‑ about the United States of America, and we don’t want to f‑‑‑ with them unless we absolutely have to. No more meetings, no more bulls‑‑‑,” Carville said in a Monday clip of the “Politics War Room” podcast.

The New York Times reported Sunday that Kushner and Jeffries met privately before the upcoming midterm elections to find common ground on issues such as housing, immigration and the cost of living.

According to Jeffries, Kushner reached out to him first, and he accepted the invitation in order to talk about affordability. Jeffries also said that the Trump administration has received pressure from House Democrats on issues like tariffs, the Affordable Care Act, and nutritional assistance.

On Monday, Jeffries, following backlash for his meeting with Kushner, wrote “no one from the Trump Cartel is getting a pass” in a post on the social platform X.

“I shouldn’t have to say it, but I am. No one is going to get a pass,” he said. “We’re going to follow the facts, apply the law, and be guided by the Constitution beginning on day one. And hold the crooks accountable.”

Former Obama aide and co-host of “Pod Save America” Tommy Vietor on Sunday criticized Kushner in reaction to the meeting.

“Jared Kushner has no actual government job; he just uses his family connections to get money from Gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals,” Vietor said.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: Supreme Court throws election curveball
articles.summary: Plus:🍁 Canada fires back ‘dollar-for-dollar’ {beacon} It’s Tuesday, the last one in the month of August. 🎵 Queue Noah Kahan’s “End of August”🎵 In today’s issue: Supreme Court’s mail-in voting ruling South Carolina, Oklahoma runoffs USS Lincoln finally heads to port Lake America? Programming note: We’re Joshua Feldstein and Claire Leibowitz, filling in…
articles.body:
It’s Tuesday, the last one in the month of August. 🎵 Queue Noah Kahan’s “End of August”🎵

Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Claire Leibowitz , filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com and cleibowitz@thehill.com .

The Supreme Court on Monday lifted a block that was preventing President Trump’s mail voting executive order from going into effect ahead of November’s midterms.

That doesn’t mean the order – which would direct the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) to only send ballots to verified citizens – is moving ahead.

First of all, there’s a second injunction on the directive in a related case before the U.S. district court in Boston. Secondly, the Supreme Court did not decide on the constitutional merits of the order, it just said the lawsuit was premature because the order had not been finalized.

That’s about to change: The USPS is set to publish a finalized rule tomorrow and states are already moving to block it — again.

All eyes are now on U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani , an appointee of former President Obama , who imposed both injunctions.

The administration says it will ask the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to pause Talwani’s other injunction if she doesn’t lift it by 5:30 p.m. EDT on Tuesday.

She has previously found the administration overstepped its constitutional authority with the order, as states have the express power to oversee elections.

Sound like a “Kafkaesque nightmare”? Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson thinks so.

The Supreme Court’s junior liberal justice wrote 23 pages of her own, saying the lift “lets another shoe drop in the Kafkaesque nightmare that our precedents have been steadily creating for certain plaintiffs who seek to bring election-related challenges.”

She wrote that it “needlessly injects chaos” into upcoming elections and that her conservative colleagues had a “lack of situational awareness.”

GOP runoff elections for senator in South Carolina and governor in Oklahoma Tuesday night will test the power of Trump’s endorsement.

And it’s honestly not looking great for his candidates.

According to Al Weaver at NOTUS , multiple Republican sources have said that a Graham win over Norman is looking increasingly unlikely, especially following her mistakes in last week’s debate.

And a new poll has the race in a dead heat. The Trafalgar Group survey shows Graham with 47.9 percent of the vote, Norman with 47.8 percent and 4.4 percent undecided.

If Graham goes down, much of the blame will likely point toward her debate flub last week, when she admitted she didn’t know much about national security in response to a question about Taiwan.

“That’s the kind of thing that, if she does lose on Tuesday, I feel like we’ll be chalking entirely up to that,” Geoffrey Skelley, Decision Desk HQ’s chief elections analyst, told The Hill’s Sarah Fortinsky.

In the Sooner State, Trump-endorsed candidate Mike Mazzei , a former state senator and state budget secretary, finished just ahead of Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond in the primary.

Trump surprised some by doubling down on his support for Mazzei, who is seen as an underdog in the race.

“Oklahoma marks one of the final midterm primary gauges of the president’s political power amid his lackluster approval numbers — and it comes after five of his gubernatorial picks in open primaries lost so far this cycle,” The Hill’s Julia Mueller writes .

Mazzei’s campaign paid almost $70,000 to Trump confidant Roger Stone for consulting services, Mueller reported, which prompted critics to ask if money factored into the president’s endorsement. The candidate has pushed back against these claims.

Whoever crosses the finish line tonight is likely assured to win the November election in the red state.

After 250 days at sea, the USS Abraham Lincoln has finally started making its way to land.

Read the receipts : Texts shared with USA Today said the USS Abraham Lincoln planned to stop in Thailand after its lengthy deployment in the Middle East for the continued conflict with Iran.

One sailor aboard the ship told their relative to send them hotel options in Thailand, while another told her family member that she was excited to visit the country.

Family members of those aboard the ship said that they have received messages about food and water shortages and mental health issues on the ship, which have been serious enough to where multiple sailors have attempted to jump overboard.

The politics of it : Democrats on the Senate Armed Services Committee have called for a discussion with the Pentagon surrounding the ongoing impact the war with Iran is having on those who have been deployed for an extended period.

Meanwhile, Trump and other members of the administration have brushed off the poor reports on the USS Abraham Lincoln.

While anti-abortion groups and conservatives have applauded President Trump’s nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton for the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) commissioner, some leaders of the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement haven’t shared their excitement.

Insiders can read the full newsletter from The Hill’s Helen Huiskes . But here’s a taste.

MAHA podcaster Alex Clark told her followers on the social platform X to push their local senators to vote against Overton’s confirmation, citing the health policy aide’s part in an executive order that boosted glyphosate herbicide production, which MAHA has pushed against.

“Everyone knows she is the biggest roadblock in the admin when it comes to getting several true MAHA initiatives done,” Clark said of Overton.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), a MAHA foe who has been very critical of the Trump administration, also said that he has “ strong concerns ” on Overton’s nomination.

Pro-Overton: Anti-abortion group leaders have expressed their support for President Trump’s nomination, highlighting her calls to restrict access to mifepristone, a medical abortion drug.

John Mize , CEO of Americans United for Life, said in a statement that Overton “has the scientific and medical background that will enable her to perform an objective analysis of the dangers chemical abortion poses to women.”

🔎 Read Huiskes’s full Insider newsletter here.

➤ CANADA RETALIATING: Canada fired back Tuesday at the U.S. tariffs that went into effect last week, announcing a slate of counter-tariffs to take effect on Sept. 8.

Canadian Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said the 15, 25 and 50 percent tariffs will be on $27.6 billion imports from the U.S.

Arguably the biggest measure is Canada doubling its tariffs on U.S. steel and aluminum to 50 percent to match the 50 percent the U.S. put on Canadian steel and aluminum.

“Those tariffs will have real consequences for Canadian workers, businesses, and communities across our nation,” Champagne said of the U.S. tariffs. “Canada must respond, and today we are in a proportionate, targeted, and strategic way.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford has also threatened to cut the province’s power exports to the U.S. as well as a response.

“We power 1.5 million homes and businesses. Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes,” Ford said during a press conference.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed pushes back in Fox News interview: ‘Not here to fight a culture war’
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, tangled with Fox News host Jesse Watters in an interview Monday, repeatedly pivoting from “culture war” questions to refocus on affordability in his state.
articles.body: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, tangled with Fox News host Jesse Watters in an interview Monday, repeatedly pivoting from “culture war” questions to refocus on affordability in his state. “You want to bring up all this culture war,” El-Sayed told Watters during the 25-minute interview. “I’m not here to fight a culture war. I’m here to fight the affordability crisis that people are facing.” Watters pressed the nominee on several hot-button topics in the combative but largely jovial interview, including whether he supports abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Shariah, gender reassignment surgery, and whether “men should play women’s sports.” On the ICE question, El-Sayed painted the agency as brutal and ineffective. “You and I both know that we’ve, long before we ever had ICE, we had INS,” he said, referring to the agency that predated ICE, the U.S. Immigration and Naturalization Service. “We were able to enforce our immigration policies without shooting people in the face and the back of the head. The INS worked a lot better.” El-Sayed added that immigration isn’t at the top of Michiganders’ minds. “When I travel the state, and I have traveled my state, more people are asking me about how they’re going to afford their gas and groceries. They’re not asking me about immigration,” he said. Asked about electric cars, the candidate said the “bigger question” is “why the president just started a trade war or escalated a trade war with Canada. It’s about to make all of our cars, especially the internal combustion engine cars, so much more expensive.” El-Sayed used that same question to advocate for hiking taxes on people making over $100 million. “Do you want to drive on good roads, or would you rather have a billionaire make a second billion? That’s what Mike Rogers wants,” he said, referring to his Republican opponent. “That’s what Donald Trump wants. Apparently, that’s what you want. I think the people in Michigan want something different. They want good roads and good schools.” “I just think I have the right to the fruits of my own labor,” Watters responded. El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim senator if elected in November, took a more libertarian tack when pushed on religious laws for Muslims and transgender issues. “So, canon law is the name for Christian law,” he said. “I don’t begrudge you your right to practice your faith as you choose. I don’t know why the idea that I could practice my faith as I choose is a problem. Nobody is trying to push Shariah law on anyone else. Just like I hope nobody is trying to push canon law on anybody else, because we live in an America where you should have the freedom of your religion.” “The issue that people are worried about is not that somehow somebody’s going to come and push Shariah law on them,” he continued. “The issue in Michigan is people are worried about how they’re going to afford their gas. The issue in Michigan is ‘How am I going to see a doctor when I get sick?’ ‘How am I going to keep my job?’” After a brief exchange on whether El-Sayed thinks the NFL is racist, prompting him to simply complain about high ticket prices, Watters then asked, “Sex changes for minors, do you support that?” “I just think the government shouldn’t tell you what kind of healthcare you should have,” El-Sayed answered. When the news anchor asked if the candidate thinks “it’s OK for a parent to slash his kid’s ding-a-ling off,” he responded, “Do you really want to have this conversation? Are you circumcised?” Watters answered in the affirmative and called it a “personal question.” “It’s a problem that you think that you get to decide what happens between a parent, a doctor and a patient,” El-Sayed said. “I’m just saying that yes, circumcision is surgery on a kid’s ding-a-ling. So if you really want to bring that up, you can. I just think you guys are really selective about these things.” Watters called the response “wacky” and “sick stuff.” On whether men should “play women’s sports,” El-Sayed said he thinks that also is not an issue for the government. “At the end of the day, the decision of who gets to play what sports ought to be decided by the people who govern sports,” he responded. “I’m running for U.S. Senate, Jesse. It’s insane. I’m out here trying to take on, like, the healthcare crisis and Big Pharma, and you’re asking me about who gets to play what sports.” Watters wrapped up the interview by thanking El-Sayed for coming on and saying he’d be invited back. “You seem a little naive, Abdul. I give you credit for facing the music, but some of the stuff’s just straight-up wacky,” Watters said. “You know, I don’t know if that’s going to fly in Michigan.”

articles.title: Democrat jabs Trump over Lake Ontario threat: ‘Let’s just call it Lake Natalie’
articles.summary: Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) on Tuesday took a jab at President Trump over his threat to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America amid his trade war with Canada, saying the U.S. should “just call it Lake Natalie” after White House executive assistant Natalie Harp. Dingell shared on the social platform X a screenshot of Trump’s…
articles.body:
Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) on Tuesday took a jab at President Trump over his threat to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America amid his trade war with Canada , saying the U.S. should “just call it Lake Natalie” after White House executive assistant Natalie Harp.

Dingell shared on the social platform X a screenshot of Trump’s threat written on Truth Social . The president said that the U.S. was “giving serious consideration” to changing the name of one of the Great Lakes.

“Let’s just call it Lake Natalie so we know you’ll start protecting our Great Lakes,” she wrote.

The president’s threat mirrors his executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America . Other locations in the U.S. share the Canadian province’s name, including Washington, D.C.’s own Ontario Road in the Reed-Cooke neighborhood and the Southern California city and transportation hub located in San Bernardino County.

Democrats, beginning with Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), have taken digs at Harp after she boarded an Air Force jet with Trump upon leaving the NATO summit in Turkey last month.

The president said he was boarding the older Air Force One instead of his Qatari-gifted jet, leaving some Cabinet members aboard the old plane while he, Harp and other White House staffers flew off on the third plane.

Ossoff mocked the president and Harp during a rally with supporters earlier this month. He said that as president, Trump only “wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”

Republican lawmakers clapped back at Ossoff, with Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) calling the discourse around Trump and Harp “ super misogynistic .” The president’s son, Eric Trump, defended Harp as a “ genuinely good person ” and called the discourse around their relationship “absolute trash.”

“It’s been amazing to watch this White House melt down over this all week,” Ossoff later said in response to the backlash during an interview with MS NOW.

Ossoff also told MS NOW’s Lawrence O’Donnell that as a White House employee in a government position, Harp and other officials working for Trump should be permissible targets of political criticism.

Harp frequently travels with Trump on golfing trips and at Mar-a-Lago, occasionally bringing along a printer to pass him information in hard copy and drafting his social media posts.

articles.title: 'Not 1984': Flock cameras watching millions of Americans spark bipartisan revolt
articles.summary: Flock Safety's automatic license plate readers face bipartisan backlash as lawmakers warn AI-powered cameras threaten Fourth Amendment privacy rights.
articles.body: There's a new frontier in the national privacy debate that's uniting people on the right and left, and it's a tool that millions of Americans encounter every day without even realizing it. Automatic license plate reader (ALPR) companies have been brought under scrutiny by lawmakers in Washington as privacy hawks warn that the growing sophistication of artificial intelligence (AI) technology is testing the bounds of what ALPR devices can legally learn about drivers on the road. One company in particular, Flock Safety, has been taking hits in the media and political sphere as news of Flock cameras' misuse — and occasional success — dominates headlines. "There's cameras everywhere, people know that, but if law enforcement has the ability to monitor the comings and goings of citizens, I think that's wrong. I mean, we're not the CCP, we're not 1984 and an Orwellian society, and Americans have rights," Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital. LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS ARE TRACKING DRIVERS EVERYWHERE He pointed to a recent incident in his district where a now-former Sarasota police officer was fired and arrested after being accused of misusing Flock camera technology, using it to spy on one particular license plate over 300 times. FLOCK SAFETY CAMERAS NEED CONSTITUTIONAL GUARDRAILS BEFORE FURTHER DEPLOYMENT, TENNESSEE MAYOR ARGUES "I don't think you're gonna be able to stop these cameras from being out there, but at the very least, there should be some type of legal parameters put in place to protect people's Fourth Amendment rights," he said. ALPRs automatically capture and analyze vehicle and location data on public roads without drivers' consent. Supporters have argued that it's a critical tool for public safety that only collects minimal information, while opponents labeled it an alarming expansion of the mass surveillance state. LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS AT HOME DEPOT AND LOWE’S SPARK PRIVACY FEARS Rep. Keith Self, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital, "These cameras are well beyond an automated license plate reader today. AI has made them so capable that they are now capable of facial recognition, of seeing what you’re doing inside your car. So it’s well beyond the license plate reader…that’s the problem. Technology has moved these beyond just looking at the back of a car." On the other side of the aisle, a spokesperson for progressive Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., pointed Fox News Digital to her recent comments responding to news that Flock was updating its oversight standards. Ramirez wrote on X, "Private tech companies have amassed record-breaking profits off our pain and the use of technology for mass surveillance is a threat to our democracy, civil liberties, and privacy. Congress must stop the ever-expanding surveillance state." ‘DARTH VADER’ USES DARK SIDE TO MOCK CONTROVERSIAL SURVEILLANCE CAMERAS: 'THE EMPEROR IS A FAN OF FLOCK' The debate even exploded onto the campaign trail ahead of November's midterm elections, where ALPRs join AI data centers as Big Tech's big boogeymen. "I oppose Flock’s mass surveillance technology, and I’ll stand with anyone in Congress, regardless of party, who wants to put limits on unchecked mass surveillance on the American people," Will Lawrence, a Democrat running for the House in Michigan's 7th Congressional District, told Fox News Digital. DSA CANDIDATE PUSHES FEDERAL AI DATA CENTER MORATORIUM WITH MICHIGAN EARLY VOTING UNDERWAY Abdul El-Sayed, the insurgent progressive Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, accused his opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich., of supporting Flock cameras in a campaign video released on X. "There's been this mass proliferation of black cameras, any and everywhere, little cameras, watching your every move to collect information about you without you even noticing," he said in the video. "If you believe, like me, that you shouldn't just be surveilled because you're driving along the street, then I hope I can earn your support." A spokesperson for Rogers told Fox News Digital that he "vehemently opposes unchecked use of Flock cameras to track law-abiding citizens. Security and liberty aren’t enemies. Good government protects both." Back on Capitol Hill, the furor over these cameras has prompted a flurry of legislative pushback. Self is among the House lawmakers pushing bills aimed at the issue, along with Reps. Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Thomas Massie, R-Ky. Steube told Fox News Digital that he's also "looking at filing something at the national level," and is sending a letter to Sarasota, Florida, officials threatening to withhold federal funding absent a promise of "reasonable restrictions" to "prevent the abuses that have happened right here in our backyard." Privacy and misuse concerns have sparked efforts across the country to cut ties with Flock specifically, from Lansing, Michigan, to Bernadillo County, New Mexico. Flock is just one company of several that operate ALPRs, some of which have been used for years. But the technology does have its benefits and has been used to stop crime. Flock Safety founder and CEO Garrett Langley told Fox News' "Saturday in America" that his technology has helped police find missing children at least twice, including after a recent carjacking in Atlanta. Flock has also said it does not use facial recognition and recently introduced new safety controls in response to the public backlash. "When I think about legislation that calls for an outright ban, that's like banning vehicles. That would never have made sense. Instead, what we did is we introduced laws against drunk driving. We introduced laws around seatbelts, laws around airbags," Langley said. "What happens if law enforcement abuses this powerful technology today? It is too often that in Flock and in other technologies, there's no regulation, there's no accountability. And we think that's wrong." Supporters of ALPRs like Flock cameras have held them up as a key crime-fighting tool, while agreeing that guardrails to prevent abuse would be helpful. "I think it's definitely a net positive. And I think that's a very easy call... the use cases and the documented cases of these things being effective tools, I think, vastly outnumber the handful of cases of abuse and misuse that we've seen," Rafael Mangual, a senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute, told Fox News Digital. "The fact that some police officers will misuse their firearms, for example, to hurt people, is not a reason to take away all police officers' firearms." Mangual said he disagreed with accusations of Fourth Amendment violations as well: "I think as of right now, these cameras can't be used to do the sorts of things that courts have recognized require a warrant." Jim Pasco, executive director of the National Fraternal Order of Police, told Fox News Digital, "There’s an awful lot of new and still developing technology out there that's very helpful to law enforcement and to enhancing public safety. That said, all of these systems need to be regulated to ensure that they aren't abused." He also cautioned against making policy decisions in the heat of an election cycle. "The most dangerous time of governance to have a crisis in is an even-numbered year, because elections are always held in even-numbered years. And I would say this problem and this year are no exception," Pasco said. "There needs to be a very careful analysis of the benefits and the risks inherent in abuse and any action that's taken should, if anything, enhance the potential for these systems being used for good and minimize the chances of abuse." articles.title: Mike Lindell misses deadline for recount payment, seeks restraining order
articles.summary: MyPillow founder Mike Lindell (R) announced Monday he will file a temporary restraining order against Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon amid his ongoing efforts to fund a private recount of the state’s gubernatorial primaries. His campaign said in a statement that Simon’s office had put Lindell “in an untenable position” by placing restrictions on…
articles.body:
MyPillow founder Mike Lindell (R) announced Monday he will file a temporary restraining order against Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon amid his ongoing efforts to fund a private recount of the state’s gubernatorial primaries.

His campaign said in a statement that Simon’s office had put Lindell “in an untenable position” by placing restrictions on his proposed audit — limiting the recount to just the two leading Republican candidates.

Lindell lost the election to Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth (R) by roughly 11 percentage points, according to Decision Desk HQ. But the MyPillow founder refused to concede, later claiming there were irregularities in vote totals .

“The rest of the candidates’ vote would not be counted under their contingent plan. Nor would the Democrat ballots be recounted,” Lindell’s campaign wrote Monday.

“Why is this important?” it continued. “In addition to being a violation of Minnesota state law, the anomalies on election night reporting identified by Mike Lindell’s team show an algorithm that applies to ALL of the candidates not simply Lindell and Demuth.”

Cassondra Knudson, a spokesperson for Simon, told The Hill that the office did not receive a payment or a discretionary request by the Aug. 24 deadline. She added that, at this time, the state does not plan to conduct a recount for the Aug. 11 primary.

In its statement, Lindell’s campaign attached an authorization form appearing to show an $825,000 transaction in progress as proof of “wire transfer readiness” for the potential audit, dated Monday morning.

The campaign is now asking the state officials to waive the Monday deadline until a court can rule on the alleged Minnesota law violations.

Knudson said that “next steps” for Lindell’s legal action against Simon and the Minnesota State Canvassing Board for their handling of the recount processes “will be decided by the court.”

“Our office provided the contingent recount plan to Mr. Lindell after it was approved by the State Canvassing Board on August 18. The plan follows state law and administrative rules on recount procedures and is consistent with previous recount plans,” she said.

The MyPillow founder currently owes the electronic voting system company Smartmatic $56,369 in sanctions following a defamation lawsuit — which his attorneys say he cannot afford. Lindell accused the company in several media appearances of rigging the 2020 presidential election, echoing President Trump’s similar false claims .

On Aug. 19, Lindell’s lawyers sent a letter to U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Bryan to file a motion to reconsider the ruling holding him liable for defamation.
